annotations.keyFindings: Interviews with 24 residents in three programmes: residents chased assessors at the end of rotations, chose straightforward activities and treated the target as a quota; some stopped asking after difficult encounters.
annotations.limitations: Residents only; three programmes; interviewer role in the programmes not described.
annotations.notes: Closest in population and question to the planned study.

annotations.keyFindings: Focus groups with 31 assessors: batch completion days after the activity, reliance on memory of the resident, brief comments because comments seemed unread; the conversation was valued more than the form.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals; focus groups may favour shared accounts over dissent.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 41,206 app assessments, 29 percent were completed more than seven days late; late comments were shorter (median 11 against 24 words).
annotations.limitations: Log data cannot explain why assessors delay; programmes self-selected into the application.
annotations.notes: Useful for describing the local export alongside interviews.

annotations.keyFindings: 46 reports: burden mostly defined as form time; cognitive, emotional and administrative burden also described; only nine reports asked both residents and assessors; none followed a change in targets.
annotations.limitations: Scoping review without appraisal of included reports; search to 2020.

annotations.keyFindings: 131 of 212 programme directors responded; median target 10 assessments per rotation; 58 percent said targets were chosen without evidence.
annotations.limitations: Self-report by directors only; 62 percent response.

annotations.keyFindings: 17 chief residents described a tick-box culture; struggling residents requested fewest assessments, so difficulties were noticed late.
annotations.limitations: Predates entrustable professional activities in the participating programmes; participants chosen by directors.

annotations.keyFindings: Reducing the minimum from twelve to eight assessments per rotation was followed by more specific and actionable comments (34 to 47 percent) and 28 percent fewer assessments, with unchanged progression decisions.
annotations.limitations: Uncontrolled before-after comparison in one programme; faculty development introduced in the same year.
annotations.notes: Relevant to what the committee may do in June.

claims.text: Residents described chasing assessors at the end of rotations, choosing straightforward activities and treating the assessment target as an administrative quota.
claims.passage: residents described spending time chasing assessors at the end of rotations, choosing straightforward activities that supervisors were likely to observe, and treating the assessment target as an administrative quota
claims.interpretation: Strategic behaviour is part of the burden the interviews should explore, not only time on forms.

claims.text: In app records, 29 percent of assessments were completed more than seven days after the observed activity, and their narrative comments were shorter (median 11 words) than same-day comments (median 24 words).
claims.passage: 29 percent of assessments were completed more than seven days later. Narrative comments on assessments completed after seven days were shorter (median 11 words) than comments on assessments completed on the same day (median 24 words)
claims.interpretation: The local 38 percent delay figure is plausibly linked to thin comments; the interviews should ask why delay happens.

claims.text: When one programme reduced its minimum number of assessments, specific and actionable comments rose from 34 percent to 47 percent and total assessments fell by 28 percent.
claims.passage: The proportion of comments rated as specific and actionable rose from 34 percent to 47 percent, and the median comment length increased from 12 to 19 words. The total number of assessments fell by 28 percent.
claims.interpretation: Fewer assessments may improve quality, but the comparison is uncontrolled; a planning signal only.

claims.text: Only nine reports on assessment burden collected primary data from both residents and assessors, and none examined how burden changed after programmes altered their targets.
claims.passage: Only nine reports collected primary data from both residents and assessors, and none examined how burden changed after programmes altered their assessment targets.
claims.interpretation: A study that includes residents, assessors and administrators together fills a documented gap.

claims.text: Assessors reported completing forms in batches days after the observed activity and relying on memory of the resident rather than of the encounter.
claims.passage: Assessors reported completing forms in batches, often days after the observed activity, and relying on memory of the resident rather than of the specific encounter.
claims.interpretation: Assessor accounts are needed alongside resident accounts.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Two qualitative studies describe residents managing assessment targets strategically (chasing assessors, choosing easy activities) and assessors completing forms late and in batches from memory. A large log analysis links delayed completion with shorter comments, and an uncontrolled before-after report suggests that a lower target improved comment quality. A scoping review finds no agreed definition of assessment burden and few studies that ask residents, assessors and administrators together. The evidence supports a qualitative study across roles in this programme; it does not settle what the target should be.
gradeRationale: Mostly single-site qualitative studies and uncontrolled comparisons; consistent in direction on strategic and delayed assessment, but transferability to this programme is uncertain and no study measured burden before and after a change in targets.
summary: Seven records appraised; five source-derived claims; certainty low.
